stances.claim: Charter change may proceed via three modes under Article XVII: (1) Con-ass with 3/4 of all members of Congress; (2) Con-con called by 2/3 of all members; (3) People's Initiative for amendments only. Each path has distinctive procedural requirements.

Where the Constitution is silent on Con-ass voting procedure, CJ's opinion is that the two chambers should vote separately (not jointly) because Congress is composed of Senate and House that 'meet and vote separately and independently' in making ordinary laws -- and 'no law requires them to meet as one body when proposing constitutional revisions or amendments.'
stances.confidence: asserted as CJ's opinion with structural analogy

stances.claim: On whether the chambers may convene jointly but vote separately, or convene separately, CJ's opinion is they may do either at their option -- given the Constitution's silence and the same structural-independence reason.
CJ encourages those who sincerely disagree to bring the issue to the SC for definitive guidance -- converting his column's IMHO opinions into a public invitation to litigate the hiatuses.

Lambino v. Comelec's distinction governs: 'revision' broadly implies a change that alters a basic constitutional principle (separation of powers, checks and balances), while 'amendment' broadly refers to a 'change that adds, reduces, or deletes words without altering the basic principles involved' -- and PI may propose only amendments, not revisions.

The 2024 Joint Resolutions adding 'UNLESS OTHERWISE PROVIDED BY LAW' to three economic provisions (public utilities, basic education, ad agencies) are 'amendments' (not revisions) -- and the House version's insistence on joint voting will kill the Resolutions because the Senate will not agree.

Two logical conclusions: (1) solons and Con-con delegates have the exclusive prerogative to propose revisions and amendments via Con-ass/Con-con; (2) the people have the exclusive prerogative to propose amendments only via PI -- and members of Congress cannot serve as concurrent Con-con delegates because the Constitution bars 'holding any other office.'

The 37-year-old Constitution needs updating because it predates 'the internet, mobile phone, bitcoin, AI, Arbitral Award, Unclos, neurotechnology, Facebook, Dingdong Dantes, Taylor Swift' -- but the path forward should be to 'proceed, with the guidance of the Supreme Court on the hiatuses, but only on the least controversial proviso, the operation of public utilities.'

notable_anecdotes: Reluctant-engagement opener: CJ 'truthfully no longer wanted to add to the ongoing noise' but friends asked him to help understand what 'President Marcos had already settled months ago.'

Lambino doctrine quoted on the revision/amendment distinction -- the same case features prominently in A77 the following month as part of the PH SC's courage-and-grit catalog.

Practical-political reading: the House version of the Joint Resolutions provides for joint voting (which would let the much-larger House overwhelm the 24-member Senate); the Senate will not agree, killing the Resolutions.

Senators-cannot-be-Con-con-delegates rule: the Constitution bars members of Congress from 'holding any other office or employment in the Government ... during his term without forfeiting his seat' -- so a sitting senator cannot concurrently serve as a Con-con delegate.

Pop-culture-modernity catalog: 'no internet, no mobile phone, no bitcoin, no AI, no Arbitral Award, no Unclos, no neurotechnology, no Facebook, no Dingdong Dantes, no Taylor Swift' -- closing the column with a memorable taxonomy of what the 1987 Constitution did not anticipate.
Recommended path: 'proceed, with the guidance of the Supreme Court on the hiatuses, but only on the least controversial proviso, the operation of public utilities' as a model for future updating.

one_paragraph_summary: Engaging reluctantly with the ongoing Charter-change 'noise' -- at friends' request, despite his sense that President Marcos had 'already settled' the issue months ago -- Panganiban offers a simple, clear walk-through of the law and jurisprudence governing Cha-cha. Article XVII of the Constitution provides three modes: (1) Con-ass, with Congress acting in constituent-assembly capacity via 3/4 of all members; (2) Con-con, which Congress may call by 2/3 of all members; and (3) People's Initiative under Section 2, requiring at least 12 percent of registered voters nationwide with at least 3 percent in every legislative district -- a double threshold that fails the PI even with 12 percent national if 3 percent is missed in even one district. He flags two constitutional hiatuses and offers his IMHO: first, the Constitution is silent on whether the two chambers vote jointly or separately in Con-ass, and CJ's opinion is they should vote separately because Congress 'meet[s] and vote[s] separately and independently' in ordinary lawmaking and 'no law requires them to meet as one body' for constitutional proposals; second, the Constitution is silent on whether the chambers must even convene jointly, and CJ's opinion is they may convene jointly or separately at their option. He encourages those who sincerely disagree to bring the question to the SC for definitive guidance. The 3/4 and 2/3 requirements are based on ALL members, including absentees -- with 24 Senate incumbents, that means 18 affirmative for 3/4 and 16 for 2/3. Under Lambino v. Comelec (Oct. 25, 2006), 'revision' broadly alters a basic constitutional principle (separation of powers, checks and balances), while 'amendment' adds, reduces, or deletes words without altering principles -- and PI may propose only amendments, not revisions. The 2024 Joint Resolutions adding 'UNLESS OTHERWISE PROVIDED BY LAW' to three economic provisions (public utilities, basic education, ad agencies -- 60-70 percent Filipino-owned) are amendments by Lambino, but the House version's insistence on joint voting will kill the Resolutions because the Senate will not agree. Two logical conclusions follow: solons and Con-con delegates have the exclusive prerogative for revisions and amendments via Con-ass/Con-con; the people have the exclusive prerogative for amendments only via PI; and because the Constitution bars Congress members from holding 'any other office or employment in the Government ... during his term without forfeiting his seat,' they cannot serve as concurrent Con-con delegates. CJ closes with a wider point: our 37-year-old Constitution needs updating because it predates 'internet, mobile phone, bitcoin, AI, Arbitral Award, Unclos, neurotechnology, Facebook, Dingdong Dantes, Taylor Swift' -- but the path should be incremental, proceeding only with the least controversial proviso (public utilities) under SC guidance on the hiatuses; if only for this, 'the noise would have served the nation.'
